# root: # Which exchange each futures root trades on, on which of its hours, and the
# size of one tick of its price: the step every price it trades at is a
# whole number of, in the units it is quoted in (grains and livestock in
# cents, Treasuries in points, so 1/64 is half a thirty-second). A fraction
# is written as one. A tick left as - is not known, and nothing that needs
# one, volume at price among them, is offered for that root. A point is what
# one whole unit of that price is worth on one contract, in the currency it
# trades in: $50 for ES, so a tick of it is $12.50. Left as -, it is not
# known, and an open position in it is not marked to the market here. The
# currency is the one a point is worth in, which is what profit and loss
# comes out in: dollars for 6E as for ES. Quoted says what the price is a
# number of. Ticks and points are the exchanges' own specifications (CME
# Group's contract specs pages, ICE Futures U.S. for the softs) for outright
# trades; calendar spreads trade in finer steps on some roots, and are not
# what a chart of the root shows.
# Months are the codes of the contract months the root lists (all for every
# month; for the metals, the active ones). Expiry is the last day a contract
# of a month trades, as the exchange's rulebook states it, and roll the
# first day the contract after it is the front month, both in the words
# 6th-bday, 10th-bday, or expiry for the root's own expiry) and steps back
# from it in business days (3b, strictly before; 0b for the anchor or the
# business day before it) or calendar days (8d). Equity index contracts
# roll on the Thursday eight days before the third-Friday expiry, where the
# volume goes over (CME's roll-dates page names the Monday of expiry week);
# contracts that are delivered roll the business day before first notice
# day: Treasuries two business days before the delivery month (the day
# before first position day), grains and metals the last business day of
# the month before, cattle the business day after the first Friday, coffee
# seven business days before the delivery month, cocoa ten before its sixth
# business day, cotton five; energy, hogs, sugar and FX, which settle or
# deliver after their last trade, roll a few business days before it.
# One exchange keeps different hours for different products: the CME's
# livestock closes at lunchtime while its equity index contracts trade all
# night. A root not listed here is taken to be on Globex's equity index hours,
# which is what most of what gets charted keeps.
